newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Aluminium to average $1,650 in 1997 - ING analyst.
newsitem.headline: Aluminium to average $1,650 in 1997 - ING analyst.

text.p: World aluminium prices are expected to average $1,650 a tonne in 1997, six percent above the estimated 1996 level, as demand edges higher and production stays mostly flat, analyst Quirijn Mulder of ING Barings said in a November research note.

"We expect demand to increase by about three percent in 1997 and production to either stagnate or edge up marginally. That implies a restoration of the supply/demand balance and consequently higher capacity utilisation rates," he said in an equity report on Dutch steel and aluminium group Hoogovens.
The 1996 estimated average price was $1,550 a tonne.
Longer-term the price should range between $1,400 and $1,800 with "occasional excursions below $1,000 and above $2,000".
At 1245 GMT three months aluminium on the London Metal Exchange was quoted at around $1,431 a tonne.

"Gradually, we believe producers in developing countries with low wage costs and/or energy prices will take over production from the more expensive countries, which will tend to drive aluminium prices down," it said.

Europe in particular would suffer under this geographical shift as wage, energy and environmental costs took their toll. "In the long run we do not expect the continuation of (primary) aluminium production in Europe."
Mulder said this development was still some 15 to 20 years away.

"Swelling worldwide trade flows and lower international transport costs could encourage this exodus as they provide easier access to raw materials (alumina) and customers (extrusion companies etc)," the report noted.
It also said the aluminium market was likely to be in balance up until the end of the year 2000, with capacity and underlying consumption growth limited to an annual three percent.

World downstream capacity (for rolled and extruded products) was expected to grow by between four and five percent a year and in Europe Mulder saw competition heating up, with Alcan expanding its German capacity and Alcoa acquiring Alumix's activities.
"Both moves are aimed at strengthening these companies' European positions," he said.
In addition, market transparency was expected to improve due to advances in information technology and the development of contracts with LME prices built in.

"This could put a permanent squeeze on margins of primary metal producers and probably benefit end-users. Overall, with LME prices in the range of $1,400 to $1,800 a tonne, we believe the downstream returns over the next few years will only be modest," the report concluded.
